item.title: Epithelial NF-κB shapes protective Treg cell responses to restrain intestinal inflammation
item.dc:creator: Luisa Barleben
Antony Julián Schneegans
Bora Uyar
Alix Bruneau
Giomar Vasileva
Franziska Flohr
Eleni Kabrani
Thomas Vasilakis
item.description:
Authors: Luisa Barleben, Antony Julián Schneegans, Bora Uyar, Alix Bruneau, Giomar Vasileva, Franziska Flohr, Eleni Kabrani, Thomas Vasilakis, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10956
Abstract: Abstract Inflammation resolution depends on coordinated communication between tissue compartments, yet how the intestinal epithelium shapes its immune microenvironment remains poorly understood. Here, using colonic biopsies from patients with ulcerative colitis (UC) and mouse models enabling tissue-wide visualization of NF-κB activity, we combine single-cell RNA sequencing and secretome analysis to define epithelial communication during colitis. We show that, paradoxically, the NF-κB-driven pro-inflammatory secretome of intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) is essential for recovery and prevents unrestrained inflammation. Mechanistically, epithelial NF-κB promotes CCL22-dependent regulatory T cell (Treg cell) recruitment and promotes a tolerogenic, pro-repair cell state, accompanied by induction of the lipid-metabolism-associated GDPD3 and CCR4. In UC, epithelial NF-κB is not uniformly activated but instead induces a selective pro-inflammatory transcriptional program while repressing targets regulating T cell recruitment. Thus, we identify dynamic epithelial–immune communication and demonstrate a protective IEC NF-κB–Treg cell axis important for resolution of intestinal inflammation.

item.title: Identification and genetic characterization of megabase-scale plasmids of Enterobacteriaceae
item.dc:creator: Allison K. Guitor
Shuai Wang
Owen T. Tuck
Brian Firek
Nadja Mostacci
April Jauhal
Lin-Xing Chen
Agata H. Dziegiel
item.description:
Authors: Allison K. Guitor, Shuai Wang, Owen T. Tuck, Brian Firek, Nadja Mostacci, April Jauhal, Lin-Xing Chen, Agata H. Dziegiel, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Humans and animals are ubiquitously colonized by Enterobacteriaceae , including both commensals and clinically significant pathogens. Here, we report 21 complete Enterobacteriaceae megaplasmid genomes of up to 1.58 Mbp in length spanning two major clades that are highly divergent from previously described plasmids. Of these, three were reconstructed from isolates of Escherichia coli and Shigella flexneri ; others were potentially hosted by species of Citrobacter and Enterobacter . Related megabase-scale plasmids were detected in at least 400 infant and adult gut, and other microbiomes. Diverse Enterobacteriaceae hosts, conjugation machinery, and DNA modification patterns suggest that these elements are self-transmissible, with a broad host range. The plasmids encode multi-drug efflux systems and potential secreted effectors. Up to 208 tRNAs are encoded and include sequence variants that may counter tRNA-centric defense mechanisms. Overall, the vast plasmid coding capacity may broaden host range, increase competitiveness, control invasion by other elements, and counter programmed cell death.

item.title: G-quadruplex structures affect the immune response to bacterial infection in mouse macrophages
item.dc:creator: Philipp Schult
Melanie Kastl
Jennifer Szlapa
Konstantinos Symeonidis
Salie Maasewerd
Bernardo Franklin
Alea Radcke
Stefan A. Juranek
item.description:
Authors: Philipp Schult, Melanie Kastl, Jennifer Szlapa, Konstantinos Symeonidis, Salie Maasewerd, Bernardo Franklin, Alea Radcke, Stefan A. Juranek, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10955
Abstract: Abstract Macrophages orchestrate immunity via transcriptional reprogramming, largely controlled by the master regulator NF-κB. However, mechanisms of promoter selection remain enigmatic. Here, we reveal that DNA secondary structures called G-quadruplexes (G4s) modulate the macrophage transcriptome during inflammation. By investigating the G4 ligand pyridostatin (PDS) in lipopolysaccharide-stimulated macrophages, we establish that G4 stabilization significantly decreases the inflammatory response without affecting mitochondrial metabolism or pathogen clearance. Instead, NF-κB-dependent transcription of activation markers and proinflammatory cytokines is selectively repressed. Using chromatin accessibility profiling, NF-κB ChIP, and in silico predictions, we demonstrate that G4 stabilization sterically hinders NF-κB promoter occupancy. Furthermore, PDS stabilizes transient, transcription-induced G4s, prematurely shutting down transcription and reverting local chromatin to a dormant state. Thus, G4 formation represents a potential strategy to modulate dysregulated macrophage activation.

item.title: Terahertz field-induced giant symmetry modulations in a van der Waals antiferromagnet
item.dc:creator: Sheikh Rubaiat Ul Haque
Martin J. Cross
Sangeeta Rajpurohit
Jonah B. Haber
Christopher J. Ciccarino
Alexandra C. Zimmerman
Isabelle J. Sealey
Vadym Kulichenko
item.description:
Authors: Sheikh Rubaiat Ul Haque, Martin J. Cross, Sangeeta Rajpurohit, Jonah B. Haber, Christopher J. Ciccarino, Alexandra C. Zimmerman, Isabelle J. Sealey, Vadym Kulichenko, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Strong-field terahertz (THz) excitations enable dynamic control over electronic, lattice and symmetry degrees of freedom in quantum materials. Here, we uncover pronounced terahertz-induced symmetry modulations and coherent phonon dynamics in the van der Waals antiferromagnet MnPS 3 , in which inversion symmetry is broken by its antiferromagnetic spin configuration. Our time-resolved second harmonic generation measurements reveal long-lived giant oscillations in the antiferromagnetic phase, with amplitudes comparable to the equilibrium signal, driven by phonons involving percent-level atomic displacements relative to the equilibrium bond lengths. The temporal evolution of the rotational anisotropy patterns indicates a dynamic breaking of mirror symmetry, modulated by two vibrational modes at 1.7 THz and 4.5 THz, with the former corresponding to a hidden mode not observed in equilibrium spectroscopy. These effects arise in part from a field-induced charge rearrangement mechanism that lowers the local crystal symmetry and couples to the phonon modes. We uncover a long-lived field-driven response with a complex THz polarization dependence, consistent with a metastable state of reduced symmetry. Through comparison with simulations, we interpret this response in terms of a potential antiferromagnetic-to-ferrimagnetic transition. Our results establish an effective field-tunable pathway for driving excitations otherwise weak in equilibrium.

item.title: Comprehensive spectroscopic analysis of energy inversion of the lowest singlet and triplet excited states in the heptazine HzTFEX2
item.dc:creator: Carolina Francener
Hector Miranda-Salinas
Christopher J. Riggs
Naoya Aizawa
Andrew Monkman
item.description:
Authors: Carolina Francener, Hector Miranda-Salinas, Christopher J. Riggs, Naoya Aizawa, Andrew Monkman
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Detailed photophysical measurements of the non-symmetric heptazine, HzTFEX 2 , previously reported as having inverted S 1 -T 1 levels, show complex behaviour, highly dependent on environment, concentration and aggregation. Here we show that, single crystals of HzTFEX 2 show anti-Kasha S 0 ←S 2 and excimer emission. Solution state absorption shows a hypsochromic shift of the π-π* S 0 →S 1 , linearly dependent on solvent polarizability. In most environments, emission is dominated by excimer species, only in toluene and frozen 2-MeTHF do monomeric properties dominate. In frozen solutions, aggregation phenomena are solvent dependent. Given such complexity, time-dependent emission spectra are crowded, making it difficult to resolve monomeric phosphorescence. However, by exciting S 0 →S 2 at 77 K, we observe a consistent phosphorescence signal at 425 nm, 110 ± 20 meV above the S 0 ←S 1 emission, whereas exciting S 0 →S 1 does not give phosphorescence or delayed fluorescence (DF). We conclude that coupling between S 2 and S 1 is very weak, S 2 -T N intersystem crossing is effective, whereas S 1 ↔T 1 intersystem crossing is thermally activated, fulfilling the conditions required for the observation of inverted phosphorescence. At room temperature, no long-lived DF is observed because exothermic T 1 →S 1 ISC becomes allowed, such that in an OLED, high efficiency can be achieved.

item.title: Terahertz emission by X-ray difference-frequency generation
item.dc:creator: N. Kida
T. Togashi
K. Tono
Y. Ikemoto
K. Sawada
item.description:
Authors: N. Kida, T. Togashi, K. Tono, Y. Ikemoto, K. Sawada
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Nonlinear interactions between X-rays and matter represent a new frontier in ultrafast science. However, X-ray difference-frequency generation (DFG)—a fundamental second-order nonlinear optical process—has not been experimentally observed until now. Here, we report the first observation of terahertz emission induced by hard X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL) pulses in solids, providing evidence for X-ray DFG. Using 10-fs, 10-keV XFEL pulses incident on ZnTe, we detected terahertz emission arising from wave mixing between different spectral components within the XFEL bandwidth. The emitted terahertz waves originate from second-order nonlinear polarization evolving on a femtosecond timescale. The polarization and angular dependences of the terahertz emission confirm that X-ray DFG is mediated not only by DFG without spatial inversion symmetry but also by DFG with spatial inversion symmetry. Quantitative analysis yields a DFG susceptibility ratio of the former to the latter of 58±4%, and the generation efficiency for 10 keV excitation is approximately 1% of that for near-infrared 1.55 eV excitation in the 100-μm-thick ZnTe crystal, while the intrinsic response normalized by interaction length is comparable. These results establish XFEL-induced terahertz emission as a general platform for probing second-order X-ray nonlinearities and ultrafast polarization dynamics in solids.

item.title: Peripheral glia drive the initiation of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
item.dc:creator: Sofia Micheli
Adrian Salas-Bastos
Khanh Huỳnh
Virginia Cecconi
Isabel Kolm
Jelena Vasilevska
Julien Debbache
Peter F. Renz
item.description:
Authors: Sofia Micheli, Adrian Salas-Bastos, Khanh Huỳnh, Virginia Cecconi, Isabel Kolm, Jelena Vasilevska, Julien Debbache, Peter F. Renz, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Although tumor innervation is known to promote cancer progression, underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood and have mostly been linked to axonal signaling. Here, we identify peripheral glia as critical drivers of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), the second most common skin cancer in humans. Tumor-associated glial cells (TAGs) resemble embryonic Schwann cell lineage stages, are abundant in the stroma of premalignant lesions and established murine and human cSCC, and are essential for tumor formation. TAG activation in premalignant lesions is triggered by UV-induced anti-inflammatory macrophages, which in turn are polarized by TAGs into pro-tumorigenic FcεRIα⁺ macrophages, key components of the cSCC microenvironment. Consequently, TAG depletion reduces FcεRIα⁺ macrophages, cancer-associated fibroblasts, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition in keratinocytes, thereby impairing cSCC initiation by disrupting intercellular communication required for tumor development. As most solid tumors are innervated and harbor peripheral glia, our findings reveal TAGs as regulators of tumor initiation with potential relevance beyond skin cancer.

item.title: A prefrontal–bed nucleus pathway controls aversive memory specificity independently of glucocorticoids
item.dc:creator: Ryan T. Lingg
Shane B. Johnson
Dalton C. Hinz
Abdullahi A. Mohamed
Timothy D. Skog
Manuela Lizarazu
Sara A. Romig-Martin
Ryan T. LaLumiere
item.description:
Authors: Ryan T. Lingg, Shane B. Johnson, Dalton C. Hinz, Abdullahi A. Mohamed, Timothy D. Skog, Manuela Lizarazu, Sara A. Romig-Martin, Ryan T. LaLumiere, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Adaptive memory requires balancing generalization to avoid similar threats with discrimination to recognize safety. The prevailing view is that stress-induced increases in glucocorticoids underlie the enhancement of memory consolidation, strengthening memories and promoting their generalization—referred to here as the standard model. However, circuits that drive memory consolidation often also regulate glucocorticoid release, confounding whether their effects on memory are circuit-driven or hormonally mediated. Here we identify a prefrontal pathway that controls memory specificity independently of glucocorticoids. Using optogenetic manipulations in male rats, we found that post-training inhibition of the rostral prelimbic cortex (rPL) to anteroventral bed nuclei of the stria terminalis (avBST) pathway promoted contextual generalization in an inhibitory avoidance discrimination task without affecting memory strength. Although this manipulation further elevated corticosterone, it produced generalization even in adrenalectomized rats, demonstrating glucocorticoid independence. Conversely, post-training pathway excitation enhanced contextual discrimination. Recordings of calcium signals revealed context-specific engagement of both avBST and avBST-projecting rPL neurons during memory retrieval, with greater responses in the neutral than the aversive context. These findings reveal glucocorticoid-independent circuit control of memory specificity, setting boundary conditions on the standard model and demonstrating mechanistic heterogeneity that may inform stress-related disorders where memory generalization is a core feature.

item.title: Oncogenic signalling and host immunocompetency govern senescent cell clearance and systemic inflammation in a mouse model of oncogene-induced senescence
item.dc:creator: Cristina Colleoni
Leonardo Ormoli
Pierangela Gallina
Laura Rudilosso
Fabrizio Benedicenti
Martina Rocchi

item.description:
Authors: Cristina Colleoni, Leonardo Ormoli, Pierangela Gallina, Laura Rudilosso, Fabrizio Benedicenti, Martina Rocchi, Rossana Norata, Sara Degl’Innocenti, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Senescence is a stress-induced program defined by permanent cell-cycle arrest and a pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Defective clearance of senescent cells promotes inflammation, tissue dysfunction, and ageing, yet determinants of their elimination remain poorly understood. Here, we model oncogene-induced senescence in the hematopoietic system by transplanting Braf V600E - or Braf ΔN -expressing hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells into recipients with distinct immune backgrounds. Braf V600E induces a stronger senescence program and more aggressive disease than Braf ΔN . Survival depends on oncogene-expressing cell burden and host immunity: immunocompetent, lower-burden mice clear oncogene-expressing cells and survive long-term, whereas higher-burden mice show checkpoint upregulation, T-cell exhaustion, and early death. NSG, Rag1KO, and lymphocyte-depleted hosts fail to clear these cells, developing sustained inflammation and bone marrow failure. Rapamycin administration attenuates senescence-associated features and improves survival. These findings identify oncogenic intensity and adaptive immune competence as coupled determinants of senescent-cell fate, with implications for chronic inflammation and senescence-targeted therapies.

item.title: High-risk antimicrobial resistance genomic traits in multidrug-resistant Salmonella across China’s food chain: projections to 2050
item.dc:creator: Michelle Baker
Xin Lu
Chengchang Luo
Ge Wu
Alexandre Maciel-Guerra
Komkiew Pinpimai
Ming Luo
Mengyu Wang
item.description:
Authors: Michelle Baker, Xin Lu, Chengchang Luo, Ge Wu, Alexandre Maciel-Guerra, Komkiew Pinpimai, Ming Luo, Mengyu Wang, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10744
Abstract: Abstract Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is rising globally, yet factors shaping its genomic evolution remain poorly understood. We investigated how socioeconomic, climate, and health factors are associated with AMR spread in multi-drug resistant (MDR) Salmonella enterica across China’s food chain, mapped hotspots and forecasted genomic trait prevalence to 2050. We analysed 2,536 MDR genomes from 15 provinces over 16 years, covering patients, food and non-food workers, meat, livestock, and environmental sources. A machine learning framework integrated genomic surveillance with risk assessment to identify high-risk AMR traits (clinically relevant, MDR, mobile). Regression models linked trait prevalence to socioeconomic, climate, health, and antimicrobial consumption data, informing projections to 2050. Eighty-four high-risk traits, including carbapenem, colistin, and β-lactam resistance, are projected to rise, with antibiotic use, population growth, healthcare spending, and urbanisation. Projections were trait-specific: bla CTX-M-64 and bla TEM-1 may increase up to 20%, while bla CTX-M-65 and bla CTX-M-14 remain below 5%. A mechanistic shift in fluoroquinolone resistance is projected: mutation-based resistance ( gyrA 87) declines while plasmid-mediated genes ( qnrB17 , qnrS1 ) rise. Food workers emerged as a potential reservoir, showing higher trait prevalence than food sources, uniquely carrying last-resort antibiotic-resistance genes ( bla TEM-30 , bla NDM-5 , bla CTX-M-64 ). Integrating genomic with socioeconomic surveillance could shift AMR interventions from reactive to preventive.

item.title: Strong field spectroscopy of many-body interactions in solids
item.dc:creator: Viacheslav Korolev
Thomas Lettau
Vipin Krishna
Alexander Croy
Martin Thümmler
Michael Zürch
Christian Spielmann
Maria Wächtler
item.description:
Authors: Viacheslav Korolev, Thomas Lettau, Vipin Krishna, Alexander Croy, Martin Thümmler, Michael Zürch, Christian Spielmann, Maria Wächtler, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10954
Abstract: Abstract High-order harmonic generation (HHG) in solids offers a promising route to compact ultrafast sources of quantum light, but its efficiency and coherence are limited by ultrafast dephasing of laser-driven electron–hole polarization. Although widely described by a phenomenological coherence time, the microscopic origin of this dephasing has remained unresolved. Here, we combine wavelength-dependent HHG measurements in monolayer and bulk semiconductors with ab initio many-body calculations of electron–phonon scattering and strong-field simulations. We show that the measured wavelength scaling of the HHG yield is quantitatively reproduced only when semiconductor Bloch equations incorporate momentum-dependent dephasing derived from first principles scattering rates. The calculations reveal that strong-field-driven carriers rapidly enter regions of the Brillouin zone with enhanced electron–phonon scattering, giving rise to effective few-femtosecond dephasing. Our results establish a microscopic foundation for dephasing in solid-state HHG and provide a framework for engineering coherence in strongly driven solids for quantum photonic applications.

item.title: Closed-loop photoreactor design enabled by machine learning and digital twins
item.dc:creator: Jasper H. A. Schuurmans
Miguel Claros
Elia Savino
Florian Lukas
Aidan Slattery
Timothy Noël
item.description:
Authors: Jasper H. A. Schuurmans, Miguel Claros, Elia Savino, Florian Lukas, Aidan Slattery, Timothy Noël
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Designing efficient photoreactors remains challenging due to the complex interplay of reflection, scattering, and absorption. Here, we introduce a closed-loop workflow integrating ray-tracing digital twins with multi-objective Bayesian optimization to design photoreactors with high photon capture and uniform irradiation. A digital 3D reactor model is calibrated using measured emission characteristics, reflectivity data, and geometrical properties and validated against potassium ferrioxalate actinometry. The validated model explores reflector shape and vial positioning, identifying geometries that maximize incident photon flux while maintaining homogeneity across 16 vials. Experimental validation using a photocatalytic Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling shows that reaction yields track simulated photon flux. The optimized reactor is further applied to quantum-yield screening, enabling mechanistic insights across diverse conditions in a single experiment. This work establishes an experimentally validated virtual co-design framework in which machine learning and digital twins accelerate photoreactor development and support quantitative understanding of photochemical processes.

item.title: Nuclear adaptation to intracellular mechanical forces regulates the phagocytic capacity of Drosophila macrophages in vivo
item.dc:creator: Clelia Amato
Rosina Graham
Rosalind Heron
Sebastian Rogatti
Christopher J. Anderson
Stephen J. Jenkins
Will Wood
item.description:
Authors: Clelia Amato, Rosina Graham, Rosalind Heron, Sebastian Rogatti, Christopher J. Anderson, Stephen J. Jenkins, Will Wood
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract How macrophages fine-tune their appetite to fulfil their clearance role is incompletely understood. Phagocytosis exacerbates cytoplasmic crowding, but whether macrophages can sense this increase and use it to regulate their phagocytic capacity has never been investigated. Here, we test the hypothesis that phagosomes exert a strain on the nucleus, which in turn responds to the intracellular mechanical inputs influencing macrophage appetite. Combining genetic manipulation and live in vivo imaging, we show that engulfed apoptotic bodies indent and deform the nucleus of Drosophila embryonic macrophages, and that phagocytosis increases Lamin B levels. Importantly, we show that silencing Lamin B or components of the LINC complex negatively regulates apoptotic body engulfment in vivo. Thus, we demonstrate that phagosome-induced nuclear molecular and mechanical adaptations are critical for Drosophila embryonic macrophages to sustain apoptotic corpse uptake, thereby unveiling a role for nuclear plasticity in the regulation of macrophage phagocytic capacity in vivo.

item.title: Superradiant charge density waves in a driven hybrid cavity-matter system
item.dc:creator: Luka Skolc
Sambuddha Chattopadhyay
Filip Marijanović
Qitong Li
Jonathan Keeling
Benjamin L. Lev
Eugene Demler
item.description:
Authors: Luka Skolc, Sambuddha Chattopadhyay, Filip Marijanović, Qitong Li, Jonathan Keeling, Benjamin L. Lev, Eugene Demler
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Optical cavities enable strong, long-range, light-matter interactions that drive collective ordering, such as superradiant self-organization in ultracold atomic gases. Extending these ideas to solid-state electron systems could enable continuous-wave optical control of electronic order, but is impeded by the mismatch between optical wavelengths and electronic length scales. Here, we propose a platform for realizing superradiant charge density waves in doped, driven transition-metal dichalcogenides coupled to an optical cavity. A nanoscale grating generates electric fields at large in-plane optical momenta, allowing cavity photons to couple efficiently to electronic density fluctuations through exciton-polaron processes. Using a linear-stability analysis, we determine the threshold for superradiant ordering and map out the driven phase diagram. We show that matching the grating periodicity to the enhanced electronic density fluctuations—such as those near Wigner crystallization—lowers the required pump intensity. Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract In 2023, the North Atlantic Ocean experienced a marine heatwave of unprecedented intensity and duration, raising the question of whether substantially more severe outcomes were physically plausible under comparable present-day preconditioning, and which processes could produce them. Here, we apply ensemble boosting to a coupled Earth system model to generate physically consistent alternative evolutions of a 2023-like event. The boosted ensemble produced marine heatwaves lasting up to 579 days, reaching maximum intensities of 4.5 °C above climatology and cumulative intensities of 717 °C·days, compared with 240 days, 2.9 °C and 224 °C·days in observations. Abstract: Abstract Decarbonizing electricity requires vast energy storage capacity worldwide, but constructing dedicated storage assets creates substantial capital, material and embodied carbon burdens. Electrified railways already exchange energy with electricity systems through traction and regenerative braking, but their inherent potential as mechanical energy storage remains unexploited. Abstract: Abstract Global cholera resurgence and vaccine shortage have driven the adoption of reactive one-dose strategies with killed oral cholera vaccines (OCVs). Abstract: Abstract The Kongming (Kom) system, consisting of KomA, KomB, and KomC, protects bacteria from phage infection. Abstract: Abstract Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus gattii are fungal pathogens that cause life-threatening infections, including cryptococcal meningitis. Chitosan modulates hydration and flexibility, and its loss increases chitin exposure and triggers species-specific remodeling of the polysaccharide network. In C. neoformans , chitosan depletion increased α-(1→3)-glucan content and reduced β-glucan levels, whereas C. gattii selectively lost one α-(1→3)-glucan subtype while maintaining β-glucan levels. Abstract: Abstract Supramolecular polymers are fundamental mimics of biological assemblies with diverse functions. Abstract: Abstract Commensal gut bacteria are key contributors to the resilience against pathogen invasion. This is exemplified by the success of faecal microbiota transplantation in treating recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection. We challenged this synthetic community as well as faecal-matter-derived communities with antibiotic treatment and C. difficile in a continuous flow bioreactor. Using generalised Lotka-Volterra and genome-scale metabolic modelling, we identified interactions between Escherichia coli and Bacteroides/Phocaeicola sp. as key to the pathogen’s suppression. Metabolomics and targeted validation experiments revealed that fructan-derived fructooligosaccharides, vitamin B3 biosynthesis, and competition for Stickland metabolism precursors causally contribute to suppression across multiple C. difficile strains and donor backgrounds. Analysis of metagenomics data from patient cohorts and clinical trials attested the in vivo relevance of the identified metabolic pathways and the ratio between Bacteroides and Escherichia in successful colonisation resistance. The latter was found to be a stronger discriminator than commonly used alpha diversity metrics. Together, our study uncovers emergent microbial interactions in pathogen resistance with implications for rational design of bacteriotherapies.

Abstract: Abstract Chlorine electro-oxidation represents the primary anode side reaction during direct seawater electrolysis, causing corrosion and permanent deactivation of catalyst and thereby insufficient stability. Authors: Hyunchul Park, Cheuk Wing Edmond Lam, Iwan Haechler, Thomas M. Schutzius, Dimos Poulikakos
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Loss of transparency due to water vapor condensation is a widespread problem across diverse applications such as windows, eyewear, displays, vehicles, and kitchenware. Conventional antifogging strategies relying on hydrophilic or hydrophobic coatings, based on chemistry and/or nano-topography, can counteract up to mild water deposition, but lose functionality at excessive condensation environments. Here, we present a passive approach, rationally micropatterning an inherently hydrophilic hydrogel to maintain high transparency under supersaturation. Guided by optics and wetting theory, and employing a diffusion model to calculate related timescales of water film formation, we engineer a wicking structure on poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate hydrogel, facilitating long-term sustainable filmwise condensation. Employing quantitative optical clarity measurements and visualization, we show that our approach clearly outperforms state-of-the-art antifogging alternatives, retaining high optical clarity even in boiling environments. Facile fabrication and superior performance establish our microstructured hydrogel as an excellent choice for sustaining transparency under extreme condensation.

Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract WHO-endorsed shortened, all-oral regimens have improved tolerability and outcomes for MDR/RR-TB treatment, but predictors of poor outcomes remain incompletely-characterized. Authors: Hun Kim, Jae-Min Kim, Yo-Han Yang, Xiaosheng Song, Dong-Gun Koo, Kang Xu, Yang-Kook Sun
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Achieving high energy density without compromising safety remains a significant challenge for advanced batteries. Nonflammable electrolytes can mitigate fire risk, but poor bulk and interfacial properties of such electrolytes limit their application. Here, a nonflammable sulfamoyl–carbonate electrolyte was developed, achieving a self-extinguishing time of ~0 s and stable cycling in both lithium metal and lithium-ion batteries under high-voltage conditions. The electrolyte comprising lithium hexafluorophosphate dissolved in dimethylsulfamoyl fluoride, fluoroethylene carbonate, and ethyl methyl carbonate at low concentration establishes a weakly solvating environment, wherein dimethylsulfamoyl fluoride and fluoroethylene carbonate preferentially contribute to stabilize the positive and negative electrodes, while working together to enhance the rate capability, low-temperature performance, and long-term cycling at high-voltage. Accelerating rate calorimetry revealed a delayed thermal runaway onset by 87 °C, correlating with Broadness Index. These findings suggest that preemptive passivation on both electrodes, when coupled with nonflammable electrolyte design, can provide a viable route toward safe, high-energy lithium batteries.

item.title: Coordinated control of both microtubule ends regulates mitotic spindle length
item.dc:creator: Shane A. Fiorenza

item.description:
Authors: Shane A. Fiorenza, Sheba Cheeran, Elena Doria, Iva M. Tolić, Patrick Meraldi, Nenad Pavin
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The mitotic spindle is a biomechanical structure whose length must be precisely controlled to ensure faithful chromosome segregation. The treadmilling of microtubules towards spindle poles, termed poleward flux, is involved in spindle length control. However, poleward flux velocity has been shown to be both inversely and directly proportional to spindle length, a contradiction that remains unexplained by current mechanisms. Here we introduce a model which demonstrates that length-dependent regulation at both microtubule ends allows plus- and minus-end dynamics to synchronize with one another, enabling pathways of poleward-flux-based spindle length control which rectify previous results. Moreover, our model predicts that spindle length and poleward flux velocity can vary independently via simultaneous perturbations at both microtubule ends, which we validate with protein depletion experiments in human cells. Finally, we provide experimental evidence for length-dependent accumulation of proteins at microtubule minus-ends. Our results thus resolve a longstanding paradox and provide mechanistic insight into the reciprocal control of spindle length and poleward flux.

Abstract: Abstract Many biologically important molecules are structural isomers that share the same molecular mass yet differ in shape, bonding and function. This creates an ambiguity for mass spectrometry imaging (MSI), where chemically distinct species can be indistinguishable on the mass-to-charge ( m/z) scale and therefore cannot be reliably mapped in heterogeneous materials. We benchmark these measurements against ion mobility spectrometry and observe consistent trends between OrbiSIMS transmission behaviour and ion mobility separation. These results establish OrbiSIMS as an approach for isomer-resolved MSI at surfaces and interfaces, opening opportunities to map isomeric biomolecules in complex systems where spatial distribution is central to function.

Abstract: Abstract Mass spectrometry-based proteomics with data-independent acquisition benefits from advanced instrumentation and computational analysis. Despite continued improvements, the quality of quantification may be poor for some measurements. MSstats+ translates these metrics into a single measure of quality, and downweights poor quality measurements when detecting differentially abundant proteins. The method offers a natural treatment of missing values, weighting the imputed values according to the quality metrics in the run. We demonstrate the accuracy of the resulting differential analysis in five experiments: two custom benchmarking studies with intentionally induced anomalies, a controlled mixture of proteomes, and two large-scale clinical investigations. Abstract: Abstract Hydration critically governs the physicochemical behavior of solutes in both the aqueous bulk and interfacial environments. As typical chaotropic Hofmeister ions, weakly hydrated anions (WHAs) can reshape hydration structures and accumulate at water–hydrophobe interfaces. Notably, WHAs paradoxically suppress the solubility of certain small-molecule monomers in water while enhancing that of chemically analogous polymers. Here, we exploit WHA-mediated Hofmeister hydration control to regulate polyamide-forming interfacial polymerization (IP), using the piperazine (PIP) and trimesoyl chloride (TMC) nanofiltration system as the primary model. Simultaneously, interfacial WHA enrichment lowers interfacial tension and, together with accelerated amine delivery, potentially intensifies transport-driven interfacial instabilities. These synergistic effects yield hollow-ridged polyamide selective layers with reduced thickness and high crosslinking density, delivering enhanced water permeance and salt rejection. item.title: Multimodal substrate recruitment enables CTLHMKLN1 E3 ligase to target acetylated N-, C-, and internal degrons
item.dc:creator: Sara Sepic

item.description:
Authors: Sara Sepic, Karthik V. Gottemukkala, Jiale Du, Samuel A. Maiwald, Jakub Chrustowicz, Eleftheria C. Papadopoulou, Luca J. Stier, Susanne von Gronau, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10877
Abstract: Abstract The GID/CTLH family of E3 ubiquitin ligases employs several substrate receptor subunits that recruit distinct degrons, but the substrate recognition mechanisms of the CTLH MKLN1 assembly have largely remained elusive. Here, we reconstitute CTLH MKLN1 -dependent ubiquitylation of three biochemically distinct substrates – MKLN1 itself, ZMYND19, and FAM72A-recruited UNG2, and determine cryo-EM structures of each substrate bound to MKLN1. The structures reveal how MKLN1’s discoidin and Kelch β-propeller domains engage substrates through multivalent contacts. MKLN1 recruits itself through discoidin-Kelch interactions between MKLN1 dimers, forming an assembly that competes with other substrates. ZMYND19 and FAM72A each bind to MKLN1 through loops engaging the discoidin trench domain while their C-terminal Arg residues engage the MKLN1 Kelch central channel, identifying MKLN1 as an Arg/C-degron receptor. The acetylated N-terminus of UNG2 is positioned within a Y-shaped tunnel of FAM72A, defining an adaptor-mediated Ac/N-degron recognition mechanism. Thus, our data reveal how combinatorial deployment of MKLN1 discoidin and Kelch domains enable a single receptor subunit to recognize a diverse substrate repertoire, adding to a complex picture of degron recognition across the GID/CTLH family.

item.title: Temporary carbon storage can mitigate slow-responding climate changes
item.dc:creator: Mitchell Dickau
H. Damon Matthews
item.description:
Authors: Mitchell Dickau, H. Damon Matthews
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Carbon removal and storage is central to many net-zero commitments, yet its durability, particularly for nature-based methods, is uncertain due to disturbance risks. Previous work shows that carbon storage-years (the time-integrated quantity of carbon storage) are proportional to time-integrated avoided warming, which in turn causes avoided changes in slow-responding climate variables. Here, we show that temporary carbon storage results in avoided changes in inertial climate variables. Avoided changes in 2100 are proportional to carbon storage-years across a range of storage amounts and emissions scenarios for permafrost carbon, ocean carbon, Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, ocean temperature, and thermosteric sea-level rise. By 2300, proportionality persists in some variables, notably sea-level rise, ocean temperature, and ocean carbon. Temporary storage therefore has climate benefits that extend beyond the duration of the storage, with some persistence of benefits even on multi-century timescales. We find that these climate benefits are greatest when temporary storage is paired with ambitious mitigation.
